title: Linkability of Continuous Sensor Data
description: The wearable device continuously captures sensor telemetry (heart rate, step counts, GPS position, timestamps) that could be linked to other data sources (e.g., social media, other devices, health records), creating a comprehensive profile of the user's activities and location patterns.
assumptions: Data from the wearable device could be correlated with external data sources through common identifiers or behavioral patterns.

title: Identifiability via Location and Movement Data
description: GPS position and timestamp data captured by the wearable device can directly identify the user's location, movements, and daily routines, potentially revealing sensitive information about their home, workplace, and frequent locations.
assumptions: GPS data is precise enough to identify specific locations and the device is not anonymized.

title: Unauthorized Disclosure of Health and Location Data
description: Sensor telemetry data (heart rate, GPS, timestamps) could be disclosed to unauthorized parties through insecure transmission, device compromise, or improper access controls, violating user privacy expectations.
assumptions: Data transmission or storage may lack adequate security measures, or access controls are insufficient.

title: Usurpation of User Identity via Wearable Device
description: The wearable device could be used by unauthorized individuals to impersonate the user or access their data, especially if the device is lost, stolen, or if authentication mechanisms are weak.
assumptions: Device authentication is not robust, or the device can be physically accessed by others.

title: Unnecessary Personal Data Disclosure to Companion App
description: The wearable device (P1) transfers comprehensive sensor data including GPS traces, device ID, timestamps, and exercise sessions to the companion app (P2). This represents explicit data disclosure that may violate the minimality principle - all this data may not be strictly required for the app's core functionality.
assumptions: The companion app may not need all transferred data for its intended purpose; some data could be processed locally on the device instead.
uncertainty_note: Using Dd.1.1 from context [4] as it describes data disclosure across boundaries

title: Linkability of User Movement Patterns
description: GPS traces combined with device ID and timestamps enable linking of movement patterns to specific individuals across time and space. This creates a persistent profile that could be used to track user behavior and location history.
assumptions: The combination of GPS, device ID, and timestamps creates a unique identifier that can be linked to the user.
uncertainty_note: Using L.1.1 as a reasonable node for linkability threats in Process→Process flows

title: Identifiability Through Device and Location Data
description: Device ID combined with GPS traces and timestamps can directly identify the user, especially when correlated with other data sources. The wearable device acts as a persistent identifier that links all collected data to a specific individual.
assumptions: Device ID is unique to the user and can be used to identify them across different contexts.
uncertainty_note: Using I.1.1 as a reasonable node for identifiability threats

title: Unauthorized Access During Data Transfer
description: The wireless transfer of sensitive personal data (GPS traces, device ID, timestamps) from wearable device to companion app creates a potential attack surface where unauthorized parties could intercept or access the data during transmission.
assumptions: The transfer occurs over wireless channels that may not be fully secured.
uncertainty_note: Using U.1.1 as a reasonable node for usurpation threats in Process→Process flows

title: Unawareness of Health Data Usage
description: The user may not be fully aware of how their calorie, meal, and weight data is being used, shared, or stored beyond the app's stated purpose. Mobile apps often collect health data for purposes beyond the primary function.
uncertainty_note: Using tree node U.1.2 from context which mentions 'Unawareness as a user sharing personal data' - this applies to health data collection scenario

title: Linkability of Health Data to Other Sources
description: The user's health data (calories, meals, weight) could potentially be linked to other data sources or used to create a comprehensive health profile, enabling inference of additional sensitive information.
uncertainty_note: Tree node L.1.1 chosen based on standard LINDDUN Pro threat tree for linkability concerns

title: Identifiability from Health Data Patterns
description: The combination of weight entries, meal logs, and calorie data could potentially identify the user, especially if combined with other data sources or if the data is unique to the individual.
uncertainty_note: Tree node I.1.1 chosen based on standard LINDDUN Pro threat tree for identifiability concerns

title: Unauthorized Disclosure of Health Data
description: There is a risk that the user's health data could be disclosed to unauthorized parties through the app, either through data breaches, improper access controls, or third-party sharing.
uncertainty_note: Tree node D.1.1 chosen based on standard LINDDUN Pro threat tree for disclosure concerns

title: Unintended Location Data Disclosure to Third Parties
description: GPS location traces with timestamps written to the location history store may be disclosed to unauthorized third parties or accessible beyond intended scope, violating the minimality principle. Location data is highly sensitive personal data that reveals movement patterns, routines, and potentially sensitive locations (home, workplace, healthcare facilities).
assumptions: The location history store may have broader access than intended, or the data may be shared with third parties without explicit consent.
uncertainty_note: Tree node Dd.1.1 is a reasonable choice for data disclosure threats in Process→DataStore flows based on LINDDUN Pro methodology.

title: Identification from Location Traces
description: GPS location data with timestamps can be used to identify individuals and their movements, revealing personal habits, routines, and associations. Even without explicit identifiers, location patterns can uniquely identify individuals and their daily activities.
assumptions: Location data is inherently identifying when combined with timestamps and can be cross-referenced with other data sources.
uncertainty_note: Tree node I.1.1 is a standard identification threat node for Process→DataStore flows.

title: Linkability of Location Data Across Time and Contexts
description: Location traces can be linked across different time periods and contexts to build comprehensive profiles of user behavior. This enables tracking of movements, associations, and potentially inferring sensitive information about the user's life.
assumptions: Location data can be correlated with other data sources or used to infer additional information about the user.
uncertainty_note: Tree node L.1.1 is appropriate for linkability threats in Process→DataStore flows.

title: Location Data Integrity Compromise
description: GPS location traces stored in the location history store could be altered, corrupted, or tampered with, leading to inaccurate location records. This could affect downstream processes that rely on accurate location data.
assumptions: The location history store may not have adequate integrity controls, or data could be modified by unauthorized actors.
uncertainty_note: Tree node D.1.1 is a standard data integrity threat node for Process→DataStore flows.

title: Unintended Health Data Disclosure to Analytics Service
description: Health log data (calorie, weight, exercise) is transferred from DataStore to Analytics Service for health-condition analysis. This represents an explicit data disclosure across a boundary. Risk: disclosure may be broader than necessary if analytics service doesn't strictly require all log types, or if data is subsequently shared beyond intended recipients.
assumptions: Analytics service may have broader access needs than documented; data may be further disclosed downstream
uncertainty_note: Using Dd.1.1 based on context [5] about data disclosure across boundaries

title: Health Log Data Used for Individual Identification
description: The analytics service processes calorie, weight, and exercise logs which are inherently identifiable personal data. Even without explicit identifiers, patterns in health data can be used to identify individuals through correlation with other data sources.
assumptions: Health data patterns are unique enough to enable identification; data may be combined with other datasets
uncertainty_note: I.1.1 chosen based on standard LINDDUN identification threat patterns for health data

title: Health Log Data Linkability Across Sessions
description: Analytics service reads logs across multiple sessions, creating opportunities to link data points to the same individual over time. This temporal linkability could enable profiling beyond the intended health-condition analysis scope.
assumptions: Session data is associated with same user; cross-session analysis is performed
uncertainty_note: L.1.1 based on standard linkability threat patterns for longitudinal health data

title: Health Log Data Integrity Compromise During Analysis
description: Analytics service processes health log data which could be tampered with or corrupted during analysis, leading to incorrect health-condition assessments. This could result in inappropriate medical recommendations or interventions.
assumptions: Analytics service has write access or can modify processed data; data integrity is not cryptographically protected
uncertainty_note: D.1.1 based on standard data integrity threat patterns for health data processing

title: Profiling via Health Analytics Insights
description: The Health Analytics Service (P3) infers health-condition risk indicators, routine summaries, and trend flags that could be used to profile individuals or groups. Inferred insights may reveal patterns about health behaviors, conditions, or risks that link to other data sources or enable group-level profiling.
assumptions: Analytics service has access to sufficient historical data to generate meaningful inferences; inferred insights are transmitted to the app in a form that preserves their analytical value.
uncertainty_note: Using L.2.2.2 from retrieved context as it addresses profiling through inferred insights, though the exact profiling mechanism may vary.

title: Insufficient Cybersecurity Risk Management for Health Data
description: The Health Analytics Service (P3) processes and transmits sensitive health-related inferred insights. Inadequate cybersecurity risk management could lead to non-compliance with health data protection regulations (e.g., HIPAA, GDPR), creating legal and organizational risk.
assumptions: Health analytics data is subject to regulatory requirements; cybersecurity controls may be insufficient to protect inferred health insights during transmission.
uncertainty_note: Nc.3 from retrieved context addresses insufficient cybersecurity risk management interplay with privacy risks, which is applicable to health data flows.

title: Disclosure of Inferred Health Insights to Mobile App
description: The Companion Mobile App (P2) receives inferred health insights (risk indicators, routine summaries, trend flags) from the Health Analytics Service. This represents a data disclosure of sensitive health-related information that may not be fully understood or controlled by the end user.
assumptions: Inferred insights contain health-related information that could be sensitive; the app may not have adequate controls to limit disclosure scope.
uncertainty_note: Using D.1.1 as a standard disclosure node; exact tree node may vary based on specific disclosure context.

title: Inaccurate or Manipulated Health Risk Indicators
description: The app displays inferred condition indicators (eating-disorder or diabetes risk signals) that could be inaccurate, misleading, or manipulated. This could lead to users making poor health decisions based on distorted data.
assumptions: The inference algorithms used to generate these indicators may have limitations or biases that affect accuracy.
uncertainty_note: Using Dd.1.1 based on general data distortion methodology; exact node may vary by LINDDUN Pro version.

title: User Unawareness of Data Inference Basis
description: Users may not understand how their health risk indicators are inferred or what data sources were used to generate these signals, leading to lack of informed consent about data processing.
assumptions: Users see the indicators but may not know the underlying data collection and inference methods.
uncertainty_note: U.1.1 is a general unawareness node; specific LINDDUN Pro version may have different node numbering.

title: Non-compliance with Health Data Protection Regulations
description: Displaying sensitive health risk indicators (eating-disorder or diabetes signals) may violate health data protection regulations (e.g., HIPAA, GDPR health data provisions) if proper consent, security, and disclosure requirements are not met.
assumptions: Health risk indicators constitute sensitive personal data requiring special protection under applicable laws.
uncertainty_note: Nc.1.1 is a general non-compliance node; specific regulatory requirements depend on jurisdiction and exact data classification.

title: Explicit Data Disclosure to Third-Party Cloud Provider
description: The Health Analytics Service (P3) explicitly transfers full health and location datasets to the Cloud Hosting Provider (EE2) for hosting and replication. This constitutes an explicit data disclosure across a system boundary to a known third party.
assumptions: The cloud provider has access to complete health and location data, which may include personally identifiable information.
uncertainty_note: Tree node Dd.1.1 is inferred from context about data disclosure to third parties; exact LINDDUN Pro node may vary.

title: Data Minimality Principle Violation Risk
description: The flow transfers the 'full health and location dataset' to the cloud provider. If this includes more data than strictly necessary for the intended purpose, it violates the data minimality principle. The disclosure may be avoidable if only aggregated or anonymized data were needed.
assumptions: The system may be sharing more personal data than required for analytics hosting purposes.
uncertainty_note: Assessment depends on actual data content and business requirements not fully specified.

title: Unauthorized Access to Hosted Health Data
description: The Cloud Hosting Provider (EE2) hosts sensitive health and location data. If the provider's security controls are inadequate, unauthorized parties may access, view, or exfiltrate the personal data.
assumptions: The cloud provider's security measures may not be sufficient to protect the sensitive data from unauthorized access.
uncertainty_note: Likelihood depends on the cloud provider's actual security posture, which is not specified.
